question.text:
You are a portfolio manager provided with the expected return and standard deviation of four assets. Asset A: Expected Mean Return: 5%, Standard Deviation: 0; Asset B: Expected Mean Return: 10%, Standard Deviation: 10%; Asset C: Expected Mean Return: 12%, Standard Deviation: 15%; Asset D: Expected Mean Return: 7%, Standard Deviation: 17%.
Which asset is the best choice for a risk-neutral investor?

explanation.text: The Logic: A risk-neutral investor, by definition in standard utility theory, is indifferent to variance and chooses the asset purely on expected return. Among the four assets, Asset C's 12% expected return is the highest, so it is the best choice for a risk-neutral investor regardless of its 15% standard deviation. A risk-averse investor would weigh standard deviation against return; a risk-neutral one does not. The Trap: Asset A tempts the overly cautious candidate and Asset B tempts those looking for 'balance', but both reflect risk aversion rather than risk neutrality. Asset D loses on both dimensions. The trap is mis-classifying risk-neutral as risk-moderate. Note: Risk-neutral utility / return-only asset selection is not defined in the cited NISM Series XXI-A PMS Distributors workbook pages checked (which cover risk appetite and risk profiling generally, with standard deviation as a risk measure). The framing above is presented as general investor-utility theory rather than as a workbook citation.
